Together, these findings define clinically relevant immune determinants for monitoring and guiding healthy aging interventions.

title: Skin-resident CXCR6+ memory CD4+ T cells and dendritic cells form dermal perivascular hubs that drive relapse in allergic dermatitis
abstract: CD4 + tissue-resident memory T (T RM ) cells are crucial for relapse in allergic skin conditions. However, the mechanisms underlying their maintenance and pathogenic potential remain poorly defined. Here, across multiple models of allergic dermatitis, we identified a C-X-C chemokine receptor 6 (CXCR6 + ) subpopulation within CD4 + T RM cells as a distinct pathogenic subset that rapidly induces relapse. This subset is supported by C-X-C chemokine ligand 16 (CXCL16)-dependent interactions with CD301b + conventional type 2 dendritic cells (cDC2s) for in situ maintenance. Functional blockade of the CXCL16-CXCR6 signaling pathway impaired proliferation and maintenance of CXCR6 + CD4 + T RM cells. In human atopic dermatitis (AD), CXCR6 + CD4 + T RM cells co-localized with CD301 + cDC2s in perivascular clusters even after successful anti-IL-13 therapy. These findings point to CXCR6 + CD4 + T RM cells as a pathogenic reservoir sustaining chronic and recurrent inflammation and suggest the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis as a therapeutic target to prevent relapse in allergic skin diseases.

title: The nerve rings twice
abstract: How does neural activity ignite skin inflammation? In this issue, Chen et al. show that one round of nociceptor activation builds a transient, chemokine CCL2-dependent dendritic cell-rich neighborhood, whereas a second round within the tested 3-12-h range licenses an IL-23-centered program through neuropeptide CGRPα.

title: Astrocytes go into presenter mode
abstract: Astrocytes are glial cells important for neuronal health, but their functions in CNS immunopathology are less understood. In a recent issue of Nature, Lee et al. report that CD40 engagement and proinflammatory cytokines promote lipid droplet accumulation in astrocytes and subsequent antigen presentation, boosting pathogenic CD4 + T cell responses during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.

title: Multidimensional view of immunotherapy
abstract: The introduction of immune checkpoint blockade revolutionized cancer treatments. Since then, the field of immunotherapy has expanded exponentially, both in therapeutic innovations and applicable disease contexts. Investigators across disciplines discuss how they are reimagining strategies to drive the immune system in contexts of cancer, autoimmunity, and beyond.

title: Viral deISGylation holds the key to the metabolic kingdom
abstract: The interferon-induced modification of cellular and viral proteins by ISG15 inhibits viral infection and is reversed by virus-encoded deISGylases, but the broad physiological impacts of this host-pathogen clash remain unclear. In this issue of Immunity, Zhu et al. reveal that ISG15 modification broadly restricts key metabolic pathways that deISGylation relieves to promote viral replication.

title: Regulatory B cells: Induced, inspired, and ready to soothe neuroinflammation
abstract: B cells can promote or restrain inflammation, yet harnessing their regulatory functions has been limited by a lack of understanding of how to efficiently induce them. In this issue of Immunity, Manfroi et al. identify chemical compounds that efficiently induce stable IL-10 production in B cells and demonstrate the ability of these regulatory cells to restrain neuroinflammation.

title: The narrow path to CD8+ T cell recognition of mutant p53
abstract: Shared cancer driver mutations offer attractive targets for cancer immunotherapy, but their expression does not necessarily put them within the reach of a T cell response. In this issue of Immunity, Haratani et al. identify distinct barriers to the processing, presentation, and recognition of neoantigens generated from mutant p53 that help explain this gap.

title: The matrix remembers
abstract: Inflammation can have lasting effects, but the mechanisms that drive these effects remain unclear. Adir and colleagues 1 reveal that intestinal inflammation leaves a durable imprint in the extracellular matrix. This modified matrix redirects stem-cell fate, sustains wound-associated epithelial programs and promotes persistent immune activation, establishing extracellular matrix memory as a mechanism linking resolved injury to chronic inflammatory disease.

title: Dan Kastner (1951–2026)
Lactate dehydrogenase A-dependent redox control of selective mRNA translation directs monocyte fate commitment
abstract: Monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation is a central process that shapes immune responses across diverse contexts, yet how inflammatory cues engage metabolism to instruct monocyte fate commitment remains unclear. Here, using a CRISPR-based metabolic screen combined with monocyte-specific perturbations in bacterial lung infection, we identified lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) as a key metabolic regulator of monocyte commitment to the nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2) + macrophage fate in vivo. LDHA-dependent cytosolic nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) regeneration enabled selective hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1α) translation through its 5' untranslated region (UTR) and is associated with structural remodeling of this region. HIF1α then functioned as a downstream effector that promoted the NOS2 + macrophage fate. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) further acted as an upstream metabolic priming signal that enhanced LDHA-dependent HIF1α regulation and supported this differentiation process. Together, these findings suggest that metabolic redox state regulates monocyte fate commitment through selective mRNA translation coupled to RNA structural remodeling.

title: Embracing macrophage complexity for research and translation
abstract: Macrophages are among the most versatile differentiated cell types in the body, serving as key regulators of tissue development, homeostasis, inflammation, repair, and immunity. Their functional diversity cannot be captured by fixed subsets, binary activation states, or single-marker definitions. Macrophage identity emerges instead from the integration of developmental origin, tissue niche, epigenetic history, local environmental cues, and disease-associated signals. Advances in single-cell genomics, spatial profiling, epigenomics, in vivo perturbation, and computational modeling now show that this behavior is organized through modular gene programs, so that any given macrophage state is best described as a weighted combination of program activities rather than a discrete label. We argue that embracing this modular architecture matters not only for annotation but for therapy: macrophage-directed interventions will require defining disease-associated states, identifying surface-accessible entry points into them, and rewiring the underlying programs with spatial and temporal precision.

title: NF-κB phosphorylation controls enhancer selection to shape the inflammatory gene program
abstract: Inflammatory transcriptional responses mediated by NF-κB are diverse despite similar upstream activation signals. Because phosphorylation of the NF-κB subunit RelA/p65 promotes interaction with co-activators CREB-binding protein/E1A binding protein p300 (CBP/p300) and selectively affects gene expression, we asked whether this modification distinguishes regulatory architectures underlying distinct immune functions. In macrophages carrying a Rela Ser276Ala mutation, p65 phosphorylation at serine 276 (S276) was dispensable for NF-κB binding to primed enhancers but essential for recruitment to nucleosome-occluded regions lacking pre-bound transcription factors (TFs) and activating histone marks. Such latent enhancers required phosphorylated NF-κB to recruit CBP/p300, promote histone acetylation, and open chromatin. Genes linked to these enhancers, including inflammatory mediators, were selectively impaired in S276A macrophages. Although antiviral responses remained intact, Rela Ser276Ala mice resisted endotoxin shock but were susceptible to bacterial infection. Thus, NF-κB responses are functionally partitioned by enhancer architecture: phosphorylation-sensitive sites define a latent enhancer compartment with NF-κB-dominated regulatory architecture, whereas primed sites are embedded in broader networks of lineage-determining and inducible TFs, yielding distinct biological outputs.

title: A microbiome-reactive TMIGD2hi Th17 subset is spatially enriched at the intestinal epithelium and expanded in inflammatory bowel disease
abstract: Subsets of intestinal CD4 + T cells directly recognize commensal bacteria and coordinate tolerance versus protective immunity. Our limited understanding of CD4 + T cell specificities and corresponding functional phenotypes has created a barrier to deciphering the mechanisms of mucosal homeostasis and inflammation mediated by the adaptive immune system. To address this, we leveraged an immunodominant Bacteroidetes epitope in SusC to perform single-cell profiling of the SusC-specific and total CD4 + T cell landscapes in intestinal tissues of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). By analyzing phenotypes and T cell receptor specificities in parallel, we uncovered phenotypic diversification of T helper 17 (Th17) cells in IBD and identified an epithelial-localized, SusC-reactive Th17 subset that is BACH2 lo , GZMA hi , and expresses the costimulatory receptor TMIGD2. Together, our results highlight the utility of tracking commensal-specific T cell responses to define specialized subsets of Th17 cells associated with loss of tolerance to the microbiome.

title: Human brain cellular xenografts in neuroimmunology and beyond
abstract: Human brain cellular xenograft (HBCX) models are emerging as a platform to study human brain physiology and pathology in vivo. HBCXs involve transplanting human pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons, glia, or organoids into immunodeficient mice to model human disease. These models have revealed human-specific cellular and molecular phenotypes, developmental trajectories, and disease mechanisms that would otherwise be inaccessible in traditional in vitro systems and animal models. They also provide a scalable, genetically editable framework for functional genomics studies, drug testing, and biomarker discovery. Given the pronounced species differences in microglia and other tissue-resident brain macrophages and their central involvement in neurodegenerative disease, these models also provide an in vivo platform to interrogate human neuroimmunology. In selected settings, they may help guide future cell-based therapeutic strategies. This review provides an overview of the current applications, discusses the challenges and limitations, and highlights future avenues of HBCXs in neuroimmunology and translational research.

title: T cell cross-priming by PD-L1+ type 1 conventional dendritic cells mediates the antitumor efficacy of a PD-L1×4-1BB bispecific antibody
abstract: Bispecific antibodies that conditionally engage costimulatory receptors aim to enhance antitumor T cell immunity while limiting systemic toxicity. We investigated mechanisms underlying the clinical performance of a PD-L1×4-1BB bispecific antibody. Therapeutic efficacy of PD-L1×4-1BB was largely independent of PD-L1 expression on malignant cells but waned in Batf3 -/- mice or upon depletion of type 1 conventional dendritic cells (cDC1s). cDC1-specific deletion of PD-L1 markedly limited tumor control. PD-L1×4-1BB enhanced proliferation of tumor-antigen-specific CD8 + T cells through mechanisms dependent on cross-presentation, the presence of interleukin (IL)-12, 4-1BB costimulation, and CD40L-mediated cDC1 licensing. PD-L1×4-1BB increased cDC1-T cell contacts, which promoted transcriptional programs associated with T cell activation and proliferation. Treated tumors exhibited increased infiltration and spatial proximity of cDC1s and activated CD8 + T cells. Accordingly, increasing dendritic-cell abundance via Flt3L further enhanced tumor control. Thus, cDC1-T cell interactions are central to PD-L1×4-1BB activity, with antigen cross-presentation, dendritic-cell licensing, and IL-12 and 4-1BB costimulation converging to promote antitumor immunity.

title: PD-L1 expression in germinal centers promotes humoral immunity by restricting T follicular regulatory cell differentiation
abstract: Germinal center (GC) responses generate humoral immunity through coordinated interactions between B cells and T follicular helper (TFH) and T follicular regulatory (TFR) cells. Despite high expression of PD-1 by TFH and TFR cells, the function of its ligand PD-L1 in the GC is unclear. Here, we show an immunogenic role for PD-L1 via tuning T-B collaboration to promote humoral immunity. Integrated analyses of secondary lymphoid organs (SLOs) revealed that B cell zone reticular cells (BRCs), including follicular dendritic cells (FDCs), expressed PD-L1. BRC expression of PD-L1 facilitated GC formation and enabled loss of B cell tolerance in autoantibody disease. Mechanistically, BRC-specific deletion of PD-L1 enhanced TFH cell production of Sostdc1 and TFR cell differentiation, destabilizing T-B contacts in the GC. Patient-derived tumor biopsies indicated that a tumor-infiltrating TFH SOSTDC1 signature inversely correlated with immunotherapy responsiveness. These findings reveal a non-canonical immunogenic role for PD-L1 in the GC and suggest that augmenting B cell responses could improve the efficacy of PD-L1 blockade.

title: Growth factor VEGF-B sustains intestinal Tfh cell stemness to restrict Taurinivorans outgrowth and microbiota-driven obesity
abstract: Autocrine signaling through vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-1 (VEGFR-1) reprograms T cell metabolism upon TCR stimulation. We found that mice bearing conditional deletion of Flt1 (encoding VEGFR-1) in T cells developed spontaneous obesity with advancing age. Analyses of lymphoid and metabolic tissues identified a VEGFR-1 + T follicular helper (Tfh) population in Peyer's patches and mesenteric lymph nodes. Flt1 deletion impaired Tfh fitness and reduced secretory IgA in the gut, resulting in unrestricted expansion of the pathobiont Taurinivorans . Taurinivorans overgrowth depleted host taurine, which drove obesity via suppressed adipocyte lipolysis and thermogenesis. Mechanistically, a VEGFR-1-AKT signaling axis promoted Tfh cell stemness by limiting p53-mediated senescence. This Tfh-microbiota-obesity pathway was also observed in diet-induced obese mice and in humans. Oral administration of IgA reduced Taurinivorans and alleviated adiposity, highlighting the therapeutic potential of this axis. Tfh cell senescence impairs IgA production, disrupting gut microbial homeostasis, with consequences to host metabolic disease.

title: Mitochondrial DNA abundance is a determinant of immunogenic cell death in cancer
abstract: Cells experiencing mitochondrial stress can undergo apoptosis or cell death that triggers innate immune activation. We examined the mechanisms determining these distinct outcomes in cancer. Abundant mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and high expression of the cGAS-STING pathway were features of KRAS -mutant cancers. In a pharmacological screen, MEK inhibitor (MEKi) effectively induced mtDNA release into the cytosol in KRAS -mutant cancer cells. However, MEKi also induced PRKN-mediated mitophagy, which limited mtDNA release by eliminating damaged mitochondria. Inhibition of mitophagy sustained mtDNA efflux and amplified cGAS-STING signaling. Mechanistically, PRKN-mediated mitophagy restrained mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) to limit mtDNA efflux. The balance between mtDNA and cytochrome c (cyt. c ) release defined two immunologically distinct outcomes: immunogenic cell death (ICD) and apoptosis. In preclinical models, combined inhibition of MEK and mitophagy induced robust dendritic cell (DC) activation and promoted CD8 + T cell-mediated antitumor immunity. Consistently, PRKN expression negatively correlated with immune infiltration in human cancers. Collectively, these findings provide a rationale for combination strategies targeting mitochondrial dynamics to augment antitumor immunity.

title: Tumor-to-dendritic cell reprogramming induces immunogenic lymphoid structures across cancers
